clinicalPearls: Dysphagia is broadly divided into oropharyngeal difficulty initiating a swallow and oesophageal difficulty with food passing lower down, and the history usually distinguishes the two
Oropharyngeal dysphagia commonly follows stroke and neurodegenerative disease and presents with coughing or choking on swallowing, nasal regurgitation, and a wet or gurgly voice
Silent aspiration, in which material enters the airway without an overt cough, is a particular danger in older and neurologically impaired patients
A bedside swallow screen helps identify at-risk patients, and speech and language therapy assessment guides diet texture and swallowing strategies
Instrumental evaluation with videofluoroscopy or fibreoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing characterises the mechanism and directs safe management
Progressive dysphagia for solids that later involves liquids, with weight loss, raises concern for oesophageal malignancy or stricture and warrants prompt endoscopy
Management includes texture-modified diets and thickened fluids, positioning and swallowing techniques, oral hygiene to reduce aspiration pneumonia risk, and treating the underlying cause
Decisions about feeding tubes should be individualised; in advanced dementia they do not reliably prevent aspiration or prolong life, so careful goals-of-care discussion is essential
reference.pathophysiology: Normal swallowing requires precise coordination of oral, pharyngeal, and oesophageal phases under neural control, with timely airway protection by laryngeal elevation and epiglottic closure. Oropharyngeal dysphagia arises from neuromuscular disorders (stroke, Parkinson disease, motor neuron disease, dementia) or local structural lesions that disrupt this coordination, impairing bolus transfer and airway protection so that material may enter the larynx and lungs. Oesophageal dysphagia results from mechanical obstruction (stricture, tumour, ring) or motility disorders that impede transit through the oesophagus. Age-related changes in muscle strength and sensation lower reserve and predispose to aspiration.
additionalDifferentials: Stroke and other neurological disease causing oropharyngeal dysphagia
Oesophageal motility disorder such as achalasia
Extrinsic compression, for example by a goitre or mediastinal mass
additionalInvestigations: Bedside swallow screening and formal speech and language therapy swallowing assessment
Videofluoroscopic swallow study or fibreoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy when an oesophageal or structural cause is suspected
Nutritional assessment and monitoring of weight and hydration
Evaluation for the underlying neurological or structural cause including relevant imaging
redFlags: Aspiration with coughing, choking, or recurrent chest infections, and the risk of aspiration pneumonia
Silent aspiration in a neurologically impaired patient
Progressive dysphagia with weight loss suggesting oesophageal malignancy
Complete inability to swallow secretions or acute food bolus obstruction
Rapidly worsening dysphagia with new neurological signs
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the underlying cause. Post-stroke dysphagia often improves over weeks with rehabilitation, whereas dysphagia from progressive neurodegenerative disease tends to worsen and, in advanced dementia, signals a poor overall prognosis. Untreated dysphagia leads to aspiration pneumonia, malnutrition, dehydration, and reduced quality of life; timely assessment and tailored management reduce these complications.
pitfalls: Assuming an intact cough reflex excludes aspiration and thereby missing silent aspiration
Neglecting oral hygiene, which strongly influences aspiration pneumonia risk
Delaying endoscopy in progressive solid-food dysphagia with weight loss
Defaulting to tube feeding in advanced dementia without a goals-of-care discussion
Overlooking medications and dry mouth as contributors to swallowing difficulty
management: Obtain a speech and language therapy assessment to guide modified diet and fluid textures and swallowing strategies such as postural techniques
Characterise the mechanism with instrumental evaluation using videofluoroscopy or fibreoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing to direct safe feeding
Treat the underlying cause, including swallowing rehabilitation after stroke, optimising Parkinson disease therapy, endoscopic dilatation of strictures, or oncological management of tumours
Reduce aspiration through oral hygiene, upright positioning, supervised feeding and vigilance for aspiration pneumonia
Support nutrition and hydration with dietitian input, considering nasogastric or gastrostomy feeding when oral intake is unsafe or inadequate
Undertake advance care planning and comfort-focused feeding decisions in advanced dementia or progressive neurodegenerative disease
Arrange prompt upper gastrointestinal endoscopy for progressive dysphagia for solids then liquids with weight loss to exclude oesophageal malignancy
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across speech and language therapy, dietetics, gastroenterology and geriatric or palliative medicine
